chapter: The jazz war with Leonard Feather
title: A jazz war that wiped out traditional players
summary: Hodes says the jazz war drove many traditional players out of full-time work. He singles out Jimmy Noone and says it should be stated historically.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: But, anyway, what I'm trying to say is, and hope to say, saying is that this is what we had to grow through, growing pains, whatever it was, and some of us survived it. But there was quite a few players that couldn't rise to this, and took to driving a cab or a day job or something. Drove them out of
Yeah, it was a very vicious, hurtful thing.

It was just too bad. We didn't have a Norman Granz to take us around in concerts. We had nobody. We had an Eddie Condon, who was doing what he could for the few in New York, and Ernie Anderson. This is what we had. And so that we survived this in itself, because the new age don't want nothing about that. And I'm not -- I think this should be stated historically, this is what happened. But I have no bones to pick, if I could do it without mentioning Leonard's name, that would be well with me, too. I'm thinking, it's just the historical thing to happen, we should know about it. There was a jazz war. It wiped out a lot of traditional jazz players, as far as continuing in the business as a playing performer. Just wiped them out, made part time musicians out of them, or completely out of it. And when I think of the horror, I think it's terrible. And I think especially of people like Jimmy Noone, never having amounted to what he should have amounted to. He should have been so much. To me, he was as important as Tatum was to the piano, to that New Orleans style clarinet.
Yeah, but he unfortunately died just as that rivalry was getting going.
Yeah, but they didn't glorify him while
it was -- there was no glory for him in the '40s.
